name: Secrets Management
intent: Keep passwords, API keys and certificates out of code and chat, hand them to the programs that need them at runtime, and make them easy to rotate when one leaks.
scenario: A service needs a database password and a payment API key. A developer pastes the key into the source code 'just for now', and the repository is later shared with a contractor.
problem: Secrets leak through source control, build logs, chat messages, screenshots, container images and former employees' laptops. Once leaked, they are hard to find and hard to replace if the same value is hard-coded in many places, so a small slip becomes a long-lasting breach.

howItWorks.title: Keep secrets out of code and images
howItWorks.text: A secret committed to a repository lives forever in its history and in every clone. Treat any secret that has ever been in code, a log or a chat as compromised. Add secret scanning to commits and pipelines to catch mistakes early.

howItWorks.title: Store them in a dedicated secrets manager
howItWorks.text: Services such as HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault or Google Secret Manager keep secrets encrypted, control who may read each one, and record every access. Applications fetch what they need at startup or on demand.

howItWorks.title: Give each workload its own identity
howItWorks.text: Instead of a shared password for the secrets manager (which would be another secret), the platform proves what a workload is, for example through a cloud role or a Kubernetes service account. The manager then releases only the secrets that identity may use.

howItWorks.title: Prefer short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials
howItWorks.text: Dynamic secrets are created on demand for one service and expire in minutes or hours, such as a database user generated for a single deployment. A leaked credential that has already expired, or that can only read one table, does little damage.

howItWorks.title: Rotate regularly and be able to rotate fast
howItWorks.text: Applications should reload secrets without redeploying, and support two valid values during a rotation. If rotation is routine, responding to a leak is a normal operation rather than a crisis. Audit logs show who read what.

pros: One place to protect, audit and rotate secrets
A leak of code or an image no longer leaks credentials
Short-lived credentials limit the damage of any theft
Per-workload access means a compromise exposes only what that workload could read
cons: Another critical system to run, secure and keep available
Applications depend on it at startup, so an outage can block deployments
Bootstrapping trust (how the first identity is proven) needs care
Rotation needs applications that can reload credentials safely
whenToUse: Any system with credentials: database passwords, API keys, signing keys, certificates
Teams where more than one person or service needs different secrets
Whenever a leak would be serious enough to need an audit trail and quick rotation
whenNotToUse: Public values that are not secret, such as a public key or a client id
Over-engineering a hobby project, where environment variables from a protected host may be enough for now
pitfalls: Committing secrets to Git, even in a private repository or a 'temporary' branch
Printing secrets in logs, error messages or crash dumps
One shared secret used by every environment and service
Never rotating, so nobody knows if rotation still works
